sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: Americans hate data centers. Tech needs them
sources.text: Though the midterms have been dubbed “the AI election” and a resounding repudiation of tech, it’s hard to tell what all this practically means. There’s a whole lot that’s clear, to be sure. The blue wave was massive, and in part that wave traces back to serious anti-tech sentiment, especially around data centers. It’s worth pinning this down clearly: Americans, right now, overwhelmingly hate data centers. A Gallup and UMass Amherst poll from earlier this year said that more than 70% of Americans oppose data center construction, and the Democrats capitalized (Democrats in over 130 federal and gubernatorial races ran anti-tech or anti-data center ads). Now, consider: Perhaps the greatest open question around Anthropic, on the eve of its historic IPO, is something like “Can they get enough compute, and can they manage the costs of that process?” The wishes of American voters seem to be on a collision course with the answers that Anthropic (and the AI boom) are looking for. It gets weirder: While this election was roundly viewed as a disavowal of tech, California’s billionaire tax (famously and financially opposed by Sergey Brin) seems likely dead. And while some data center stocks dropped on Wednesday (Tesla and SpaceX shares also saw non-trivial drops), the Dow actually rallied on Democrats’ victories, up 1500 points. Brin’s possible success in shooting down the billionaire tax in California has proven singular. Famously, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz were among the most active donors to Republican candidates in these midterms, to the reported tune of more than $100 million. The same was true of Musk, who reportedly donated well over $400 million. This all got a lot of press in the lead-up to the midterms, and rightfully so. But most of these billionaires were suspiciously quiet on X on Wednesday, at least as of this writing in the afternoon. Musk was notable in sounding off: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.” To me, for all the questions that remain, what these results prove goes something like this: The American people are exhausted and afraid of the AI boom, and no amount of billionaires yapping on X or funneling millions into the election is changing that. Where that takes this world of people I cover from here, I don’t know. Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . Morgan Chittum curated the deals section of today’s newsletter . - Sentra , a data security company, raised $150 million in a Series C funding round. The investment was led by Capital One Ventures , with participation from existing investors Bessemer Venture Partners , Zeev Ventures, Standard Investments, Munich Re Ventures, and Key1 Capital. - Kabilio , a Barcelona-based startup that uses AI to automate accounting and tax processes, raised over $11 million in funding. The round was led by Picus Capital and Visionaries . - Shackleton AI, a New York-based developer of an AI platform for construction management, secured $5 million in seed funding led by Battery Ventures , with participation from Brick & Mortar Ventures, Trust Ventures, Correlation Ventures, Motivate Partners, Thayer Investment Partners, Act One Ventures, Brainstorm Ventures, Silence VC, and others. - Kalepa announced a $75 million Series B funding round at a $470 million valuation. Updata Partners led the company’s raise. Other backers include IA Ventures and Inspired Capital. - Phaze , a remote desktop platform for both human and AI agents, raised $8.75 million in seed funding led by a16z , with participation from Indie, NextView, Makers, and Lerer Hippeau . - Pliant , a Berlin-based payments infrastructure company, secured $80 million in Series C funding, led by Seaya Nova and Speedinvest . Illuminate Financial, Motive Partners, and Molten Ventures also participated in the round. - Aspirity Partners committed $135 million through a strategic minority investment to London-based wealth management platform Hoxton Wealth . - Sapphiros and binx health have merged to form diagnostic company Onvaro . KKR, Hildred, and EQT Life Sciences are investing additional capital in the combined business. Financial terms were not disclosed. - Abnormal AI , a cybersecurity company backed by Greylock, Menlo Ventures, and Wellington Management , appointed Don Jeter as chief marketing officer. Jeter previously held the same role at Torq.

sources.title: The Blue Wave Has Tech Bros Scrambling for Data Centers in Space
sources.text: A wave of Democratic candidates across the country —and notably in Texas, a national data center hot spot and home to Elon Musk’s SpaceX—won their state and congressional races on Tuesday, including many candidates who voiced opposition to the data center industry . The results have sent some corners of the tech industry looking to the heavens for answers. In recent hours, data center enthusiasts have proclaimed on social media that they’re still “ bullish ” on building data centers—just not necessarily in Texas, or even on Earth at all. Instead, they say, it’s time to focus on data centers in space. Elon Musk—who spent more than $400 million of his fortune supporting Republican candidates who all went on to lose their midterms races—has been among those leading the charge. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours of Wednesday, after it was clear that Democrats had taken the House and Senate. Jordan Lasker— the man behind the X account "Crémieux,” which is a popular follow in the tech world and is known for posting race-based pseudoscience—also weighed in, saying , “Data centers in space are an incredible idea and anyone who doubted them didn't think enough about tonight's election results.” Throughout the day, Musk employees , tech investors , AI researchers , venture capitalists , and industry fans joined the chorus of support for space-based data centers. Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the techno-optimist think tank Foundation for American Innovation, argued that underwater data centers should also be considered. (In June, China began operating what it claims is the world’s first underwater data center.) Some companies are already trying to put compute in orbit. Among them are Google, which launched a satellite that it says contains “data center class TPU,” and SpaceX, which says it aims to deploy “thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027.” Blue Origin is also in the mix, having filed for a Federal Communications Commission permit to launch 50,000 satellites that will constitute an “orbital data center system.” There are also a few startups aiming to build data centers in space, including Starcloud, which claims to have carried "the first Nvidia H100 GPU into orbit" in November 2025. Despite being technically possible, the realities of in-orbit data centers are difficult . Among other things, space-based data centers are much more expensive than land-based ones, can’t grow to hyperscale size, and are subject to the risks and whims of satellite launches. When it comes to Texas data centers, the concerns of tech bros aren’t completely unfounded. Experts tell WIRED that the change in leadership could translate to some concrete changes in the industry—albeit with limits. Although Democrats will have control of the Texas House of Representatives, Republicans still have control over the state’s senate. Robert Paterson, professor of land use and environmental planning at the University of Texas at Austin, tells WIRED that the split means that some immediate attempts at change “will probably be stymied a bit.” Adrian Shelley, director of nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen’s Texas office, tells WIRED that the legislature would be a likely place to hash out high-impact policies like the reallocation of state agency resources. However, he adds that the governor could effect more immediate changes by issuing executive orders, or requesting the resignation of politically appointed officials in state agencies. Shelley says that these oversight agencies—such as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission, and the Texas Water Development Board—have the authority to charge fines for breaking state law, or in extreme cases to revoke permits for projects like data centers. But Paterson notes that Texas developers have particularly strong “vested rights,” which protects the terms of their projects from the moment their permits are approved, even if construction hasn’t begun. Another medium-term route to reshaping Texas’ data center industry could be to give more power to its counties. Paterson noted that nearly half of the state’s data centers exist in unincorporated territory, which puts them outside the jurisdiction of city zoning laws. Unlike other states, Paterson says, Texas counties have relatively limited enforcement abilities. Under the state's so-called Dillon’s Rule, counties only have powers that are “specifically allotted to it by the state.” So while they have authority over things like access and egress to county roads or construction on floodplains, he says they don't have the zoning authority that would help closely regulate projects like data centers. Paterson says that the new attorney general could theoretically adjust the terms in the state’s biannual handbook, which establishes the limits of county authority. He also argues that even in a split legislature, especially since anti-data-center sentiment crosses party lines, state lawmakers could propose a viable bill giving counties “limited zoning authority over data centers." Shelley tells WIRED that since “data centers were a decisive factor in this blue wave,” the upcoming legislative season will be “very interesting.” “I will say the data center industry hasn't shown a lot of interest in working with state lawmakers or local leaders,” Shelley says, “and I will be interested to see if that changes.”

sources.title: Google fine-tunes its Agentic Data Cloud to support highly scalable autonomous AI workers
sources.text: Artificial intelligence is no longer just about conversational assistants that tell people what to do. These days, it’s all about work automation, and Google Cloud is making sure it’s right at the forefront of that trend with its revamped Agentic Data Cloud platform, which received a host of new updates today. The Agentic Data Cloud was launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next. It’s meant to be the architectural “system of action” for AI agents , replacing the brittle extract, transform and load-based data pipelines, or ETL, that feed legacy software applications. The key advantage of Agentic Data Cloud is that it meets customers where their data is, so rather than forcing them to squeeze all of their information in a large, centralized data warehouse, it enables AI agents to access it wherever it lives. In a blog post, Sirish Chandrasekaran, Google’s vice president of product management for data analytics, outlined the company’s belief that autonomous agents rather than humans will soon become the primary consumers of data. As such, it makes sense to build a purpose-built infrastructure stack specifically for them, prioritizing low latency, zero data movement and automated governance. “That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a system of action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost,” Chandrasekaran said. The flagship new feature in Agentic Data Cloud is borderless Lakehouse , a special version of Google’s “cross-border Lakehouse” product that also debuted at Cloud Next. Chandrasekaran said borderless Lakehouse is built upon the open-source Apache Iceberg table format and designed to eliminate multicloud friction with new caching capabilities for Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. This allows companies to query remote data held in those cloud platforms over a secure private link, without having to pay egress fees. Chandrasekaran detailed how it works, saying that it automatically caches retrieved data blocks within Google Cloud to accelerate subsequent queries. There’s also a new AlloyDB integration that allows users to query external Iceberg tables with standard PostgreSQL queries without having to copy data. In this way, it bridges real-time transactional data with historical lakehouse records. One of the big problems with autonomous agents is that they can be prone to hallucinations without proper guardrails in place, which is why Google has overhauled another capability within Agentic Data Cloud. The Knowledge Catalog , which is a kind of map of business meaning that’s meant to inform AI agents of the peculiarities of the organization they work for, is getting a new self-learning enrichment capability in preview. According to Chandrasekaran, it works by continuously scanning unstructured data in Google Workspace, Jira, SharePoint and GitHub to translate operational knowledge into Open Knowledge Format context sets. These can be used to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge, and the results from early adopters shows that it can help make the average agent four-times more accurate, while reducing token consumption by up to 75%. Knowledge Catalog is seen as so important to Google’s agentic future that it’s also being enabled by default in the Gemini application starting today. Because it’s so tightly integrated, it can resolve issues around business metric definitions and access controls before it translates user’s prompts into Structured Query Language queries. Companies can also choose to ground agents in semantic models for specific data platforms, including Google BigQuery, Snowflake, SAP, Looker and dbt. “Agents are only as accurate as the business context they’re grounded in,” Chandrasekaran said. “Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on.” Gemini is also getting new autonomous machine learning capabilities that can help to streamline everyday work for both technical teams and business workers. For instance, data engineers can now tell Gemini a specific business outcome they want to achieve in natural language, and Gemini will generate the PySpark code, run the notebooks and fix any data pipeline errors as it works toward that goal. Meanwhile, business users will be able to generate reliable, real-time operational reports in Gemini simply by asking for them. “Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query,” Chandrasekaran explained. “Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent and verified answers every time.” Google also has a few gifts for software developers, starting with the new Data Agent Kit , which is generally available from today, bringing Model Context Protocol tooling into integrated development environments such as VS Code, Claude Code and Antigravity . This means that developers can now just define their business intent in natural language and have agents automatically create, fine-tune and test the associated data pipelines. Developers can also take advantage of infrastructure updates that are designed to facilitate “high-concurrency agent interactions,” so that thousands of AI agents can query the same database simultaneously without swamping it and causing problems. These include the broader preview of AlloyDB Express , a highly scalable database that supports sub-two-second provisioning for rapid agent prototyping. There’s also PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB , which provides an isolated workload environment that can handle three million queries per second. Finally, Google said BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics into relational database tables with zero ETL. sources.title: Experts warn building new data centers across the US could wipe out the last 15 years of greenhouse gas progress
sources.text: New data centres could push US power-sector emissions sharply higher The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States is creating new concerns about the country's ability to reduce CO 2 emissions. A new Sierra Club assessment warns that electricity generation associated with planned data center developments could reverse years of environmental gains. By 2030, CO 2 emissions linked to the expansion could exceed 460 million metric tons, matching Mexico's annual carbon dioxide emissions. The environmental organisation estimates that electricity demand from proposed facilities could substantially increase pollution from the American power sector before the decade ends. Projections indicate that CO 2 emissions could reach 2.1 billion metric tons, representing a 42% increase over 2025 levels. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” said Jeremy Fusher, Sierra Club's principal advisor for climate and energy, expressing surprise at the scale of the latest estimates. The organisation's earlier calculations placed the projected increase between 25% and 50% of its current estimate. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The revised assessment therefore indicates that electricity requirements associated with planned computing infrastructure could create a huge environmental cost. Natural gas remains an important part of the electricity supply supporting American data centres. Approximately 40% of these facilities receive electricity from gas turbines, while renewable energy additions are struggling to match rapidly increasing consumption. Competition for electricity generation equipment is creating additional difficulties for developers seeking to bring facilities online quickly. Turbine prices have increased by 50%, while manufacturers face substantial production backlogs extending several years. One manufacturer has reportedly opened production reservations for equipment scheduled for delivery in 2032. These constraints could encourage developers to retain fossil fuel generation rather than wait for renewable alternatives or additional electricity infrastructure. Equipment shortages, delayed grid connections and other infrastructure constraints could prevent numerous developments from becoming operational. Across the United States, applications for construction permits reportedly exceed the electricity transmission capacity available in several locations. Some projects also face opposition from communities concerned about electricity consumption, environmental consequences and the costs associated with infrastructure expansion. Financial uncertainty within the artificial intelligence industry introduces another complication for developers planning large computing facilities. Hyperscalers facing questions about the commercial returns from their investments could postpone or abandon projects before construction reaches completion. Government regulations requiring renewable electricity for new facilities may provide some protection against additional emissions. However, existing requirements frequently include implementation periods and generally do not apply retrospectively to operating installations. Ireland, for example, requires new data centres to obtain 80% of their electricity from renewable sources within six years of beginning operations. Such delays mean fossil fuel generation could remain part of the electricity supply during substantial periods of infrastructure expansion. Due to these uncertainties, the eventual impact of data centre expansion on greenhouse gas emissions remains difficult to predict. Efosa has been writing about technology for over 7 years, initially driven by curiosity but now fueled by a strong passion for the field. He holds both a Master's and a PhD in sciences, which provided him with a solid foundation in analytical thinking. sources.title: After the midterms, a bigger clash over data centers could be coming
sources.text: The November 3 midterm results gave Democrats full control of Congress, setting the stage for what could be one of the most divided U.S. governments this decade, with Republicans in the White House. Tuesday’s results suggest that anger over data centers, the large facilities that house the computers powering AI, is becoming a political force. With Democrats now in control of Congress, that could lead to new limits on where data centers can be built and how much say local communities have. Data centers became a ballot-box issue in various states. An NBC exit poll showed how concerned voters are about AI: More than half of respondents believe that AI will do more harm than good, while almost 80% are against the building of data centers in their neighborhoods. Almost 60%, meanwhile, said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote. Nadine Smith, president and CEO of the racial justice organization Color of Change, called Tuesday’s election a referendum on “who this economy is built for.” “National security matters,” Smith said, referring to a common argument from data center supporters that the infrastructure is essential for the U.S. to stay ahead in war and in its rivalry with China. “And so do the families in South Memphis breathing exhaust from the gas turbines powering an AI supercomputer.” (She was referring to xAI’s data center in Memphis, Tennessee, which uses gas turbines for power.) Voters in several states pushed back against the AI buildout, even as pro-AI super PACs spent millions hoping to sway them this midterm. The anti-data center backlash was especially felt in states like Ohio, where OpenAI has eyed a $500 billion data center, backed by more than $100 billion in financing from Nvidia. In fact, the Ohio county where Meta had planned a 700,000-square-foot facility just passed a ban on data centers, and local communities across the state overwhelmingly voted against data center buildout measures. Analysts at Morgan Stanley predict that Democratic governor-elect Amy Acton will also pose a major risk to Ohio’s data center buildout. Elsewhere, candidates in Texas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Georgia, and South Carolina all won seats after taking a stance against the rapid buildout of data centers. “It is clear that money does not buy outcomes,” said Anshi Bhatt, a tech and policy researcher, adding that in modern politics, creating a “local villain” is one way to build campaign momentum. Likely next steps include more construction moratoriums or requiring data centers to pay for their own power grid upgrades instead of passing those costs on to nearby communities. Goldman Sachs, in fact, predicts data center construction delays in states like Georgia and Texas because of Democratic gains. Democratic control of Congress could also improve the odds for bills like the one Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced earlier this year, though any such bill would also face a possible veto. It proposes a nationwide moratorium on new data centers until Congress adds new guardrails and ensures that the buildout does not raise electricity costs, harm the environment, or proceed without community approval. There are also bills like the GRID Savings Act, proposed by New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, which would prevent grid infrastructure costs from being passed on to communities during large AI data center buildouts. The environment is also a major concern, especially at xAI’s data center in Memphis and at the data centers throughout Virginia, known as the world capital of data centers, where gas turbines are used for power. Maia Woluchem, program director at Data & Society, a nonprofit research group, believes that changes to energy regulations, land rights, and other environmental policies could affect the data center buildout, especially as congressional Democrats look further into the Trump administration’s rollback of certain energy protections, as the New York Times reported they might . “Regardless of federal action, I could imagine that we will see additional movement at the state and local level, given the momentum that’s been building from the ground up,” Woluchem continued, citing governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who supports a statewide moratorium on data centers, as an example. Both Hinojosa and Gov. Greg Abbott called for some limits, but Hinojosa centered much of her campaign on opposing data centers, a notable choice in Texas, whose electrical grid has proved vulnerable over the past decade. But the hard part is still to come. Smith, for example, is now expecting a fight, or even more executive orders, to bypass what Congress is now likely to block. “Even among Democrats, a blanket freeze is contested,” she said, referring to some Democrats’ worry that a moratorium could slow AI progress and hurt national security. She also expects AI lobbyists to start calling lawmakers. “Democrats ran on making Big Tech pay,” Smith said. “Our job is to make sure they remember it once the cameras leave.” The backlash runs deeper than the buildings themselves, which aren’t new. One private equity executive told me recently that people don’t necessarily hate data centers, but rather AI, and that data centers have become a stand-in for people’s fears and anxieties about the technology. “It does look like the results are pointing to a real frustration with tech power at minimum,” Woluchem said, noting that this is also a bipartisan issue. For the past month, people have told me they are worried about data centers’ effect on the environment and about their lack of say in whether they’re built. Amazon, for example, built a data center in Gilroy, California, without many residents knowing , by satisfying a 45-year-old zoning law. Vague or outdated zoning laws, along with requirements that local officials sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) barring them from discussing data center projects, have only fueled people’s outrage about the buildout. sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Em virada histórica, AMD deve faturar mais que a Intel pela primeira vez
sources.text: Por Raphael Giannotti | 04/11/2026 às 19:15 A AMD atingiu um marco histórico no mercado de semicondutores. Na reunião com os acionistas, referente aos resultados financeiros do terceiro trimestre de 2026, o Time Vermelho não apenas registrou sua maior receita trimestral da história, US$ 13,37 bilhões , como também projetou um faturamento de aproximadamente US$ 17 bilhões para o quarto trimestre . Se a previsão se confirmar, a marca comandada por Lisa Su vai ultrapassar o faturamento da rival Intel (que estima entre US$ 15 bilhões e US$ 16 bilhões no mesmo período) pela primeira vez desde a sua fundação. Assim como qualquer fabricante de hardware hoje, o motivo para esse crescimento é o foco em infraestrutura para inteligência artificial e nuvem. A divisão de data center da AMD disparou 97% em relação ao ano anterior , faturando US$ 8,55 bilhões no trimestre e passando a responder por 64% de toda a receita da companhia . O crescimento acelerado é impulsionado pela forte adoção dos processadores Epyc e pela alta demanda das aceleradoras Instinct MI455X por gigantes como Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI e Oracle. Apesar do desempenho recorde no setor corporativo, o segmento focado no consumidor final acendeu o sinal amarelo. A receita somada das divisões de Client (processadores Ryzen para PC) e Gaming caiu 8% no comparativo anual, totalizando US$ 3,72 bilhões . O tombo mais forte veio da área de jogos, que despencou 40% devido à menor encomenda de chips customizados para os consoles da Sony e Microsoft nessa fase da geração, além das vendas mornas de placas de vídeo Radeon . Durante a conversa com investidores, a CEO Lisa Su projetou um cenário desafiador para a indústria de PCs nos próximos anos. Pressionado pela alta no custo de componentes, com destaque para a escalada nos preços das memórias RAM, o mercado global de PCs deve encarar uma queda de dois dígitos nos envios em 2027 . Ainda assim, a AMD aposta na força da linha Ryzen, que deve receber modelos Zen 6 em breve, para desktops de alto desempenho e no mercado corporativo para continuar ganhando espaço, mesmo em um cenário de retração geral.

sources.name: Xataka
sources.title: AMD va a adelantar a Intel por primera vez en su historia
sources.text: AMD está a punto de arrebatar a Intel su reinado. Durante los últimos cinco años los ingresos de la compañía liderada por Lip-Bu Tan han permanecido prácticamente estancados o han retrocedido . Mientras tanto, la facturación de AMD ha crecido notablemente, especialmente durante los últimos dos años. Para muestra, un botón: en 2021 Intel facturaba casi cinco veces más que AMD. Sus ingresos eran de 79.000 millones de dólares , frente a los 16.400 millones de su rival. En 2022 se produjo un cambio de tendencia importante. La facturación de Intel se redujo a 63.100 millones de dólares , mientras que la de AMD se incrementó hasta los 23.600 millones . Y llegamos a 2025, un año en el que los ingresos de la compañía liderada por Lisa Su alcanzaron los 34.600 millones de dólares . AMD empezaba a intimidar seriamente a Intel, cuya facturación cayó el año pasado hasta los 52.900 millones de dólares . La tendencia al alza de los ingresos de AMD y al estancamiento de los de Intel se ha mantenido durante los últimos meses. Y ahora, en la recta final de 2026, la compañía de Lisa Su está a punto de dar el golpe definitivo: sus previsiones apuntan a que ingresará más dinero que su histórico rival por primera vez. AMD prevé ingresar aproximadamente 17.000 millones de dólares durante el cuarto trimestre de 2026. E Intel espera facturar entre 15.000 y 16.000 millones durante este mismo periodo. Basta pasarse por los foros especializados en hardware de PC para darse cuenta de que muchos usuarios prefieren los procesadores Ryzen de AMD a las CPU que nos ha propuesto Intel durante los últimos años. Nuestros análisis también están alineados con esta corriente de pensamiento, y de una cosa no cabe duda: los chips Ryzen son extraordinariamente competitivos desde hace ya muchos años tanto al lidiar con videojuegos como en un escenario ofimático o de creación de contenidos. De una cosa no cabe duda: AMD ya no es en absoluto la "segundona" que era en los años 90 y a principios de los 2000. En cualquier caso, durante los últimos años las dos fuentes de ingresos que han catapultado el crecimiento de AMD han sido los aceleradores de IA y los procesadores EPYC. Estas dos familias de chips están destinadas a centros de datos, y la explosión de la inteligencia artificial (IA) que estamos viviendo ha provocado que su demanda se dispare , sobre todo durante los últimos dos años. Precisamente, este incremento de la demanda de los aceleradores para IA Instinct y los procesadores EPYC coincide con el aumento más robusto de los ingresos de esta compañía. Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI y Oracle Cloud Infrastructure ya están comprando los sistemas Helios de AMD No obstante, más allá de la competitividad de estas dos familias de chips desde un punto de vista estrictamente técnico, hay algo que AMD ha hecho muy bien: ha ideado una estrategia que persigue ofrecer sistemas completos para centros de datos mediante Helios, su plataforma de computación a escala de rack . Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI y Oracle Cloud Infrastructure ya le están comprando sus sistemas Helios. Lisa Su ha anticipado que su división de soluciones para centros de datos representará más del 80% de los ingresos de AMD en 2027. En la otra cara de la moneda tenemos a Intel. La llegada de Lip-Bu Tan en marzo del año pasado ha sido un acicate para los inversores, y los resultados económicos de la compañía han mejorado. Sin embargo, sigue teniendo dificultades para satisfacer la demanda de procesadores Xeon , que le permiten competir en el mercado de los centros de datos. Además, el mercado del PC se ha debilitado mucho como consecuencia del drástico incremento del precio de algunos componentes, y este panorama también está haciendo daño a Intel. Ahora mismo el futuro a medio plazo pinta mucho más amable para AMD que para Intel. En Xataka | AMD vs. Intel: quién lleva la delantera en la gran batalla histórica de los procesadores

sources.title: OpenAI pledges to halt NDAs in new data center policy proposal after election rebuke
sources.text: OpenAI reaffirmed its promise to pay the full cost of powering data centers as part of a series of commitments the company published Thursday, two days after voters at the polls roundly rejected the rapid expansion of AI. The artificial intelligence company said in its commitments that for data centers it owns and operates, it will solicit community input, publish construction plans and stay away from using non-disclosure agreements with public officials. Additionally, in a policy blueprint, OpenAI encouraged policymakers to enact similar commitments as laws. "What we're doing with this blueprint is really laying out the best lessons that we have learned and committing to applying them as they go forward," OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane told reporters during a Wednesday briefing. "This will help ensure that there is a very high floor in terms of how people move forward." Other tech companies, including Meta, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic , have outlined several similar commitments . On Tuesday, Americans issued a stinging rebuke of data centers at the polls. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures for all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Opposition to AI data centers mounted swiftly over the summer across both sides of the political aisle. Consumers grappling with inflation, rising grocery prices and stubbornly high prices at the pump grew worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, they became a physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy and anxiety around AI. AI companies like OpenAI depend on AI data centers to serve customers and develop new models, and they're seeking to build out as rapidly as possible to meet demand. In February, OpenAI told investors that it's targeting $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and the company has since announced massive data center projects in Georgia and Ohio . OpenAI has repeatedly pledged to protect ratepayers and invest in local communities this year, and Lehane said the company's latest commitments build on many of its previous initiatives. He said the policy blueprint has been in the works since August, and that he met with dozens of lawmakers and candidates since then. "Having these conversations now actually helps put more energy into the momentum, so that when people come back in late January, new Congress is in in session, a lot of the work is being done in advance," Lehane said.
